extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of linguistics, literary theory, poetics, and creative writers studying models of text/poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Use Roman Jakobson's theories (six functions of language, poetic function, markedness, distinctive features, and phonological/analytical methods) as criteria for analysing or composing texts—especially poetry and other literary forms. Emphasises which communicative function is dominant, the role of sound and form, and structural analytic techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referential function
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This function concerns the context or informational content of a message; texts whose primary aim is to convey information (reports, descriptions, expository writing) foreground the referential function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic / Poetic function
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poetic function focuses on the message itself (its form and arrangement). In poetic texts the organization, equivalence and patterned features of language are foregrounded; according to Jakobson this is the dominant function in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotive function
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns the speaker's/expression's attitude and emotions. Use this criterion to evaluate texts where subjective expression and affective stance are central (e.g., lyric voice, confessional prose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conative function
rubrics_metrics.description: Conative (: vocative or imperative addressing of receiver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates how a text attempts to influence or directly address the addressee (commands, vocatives, rhetorical address). Relevant for dramatic dialogue, persuasive writing, and texts oriented toward action from the receiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phatic function
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures attention to the communication channel itself—phrases whose purpose is to open/maintain social contact or check that communication is possible (e.g., greetings, small talk, interruptions). Useful for analysing interactional texture in dialogue or performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metalingual function
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pertains to language about language—clarification of vocabulary, definitions, or comments on linguistic code. Apply when a text self-consciously explains, defines, or plays with its own sign system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant-function principle
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the six functions is always the dominant function in a text and usually related to the type of text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or composing, identify which of the six functions is dominant—this will typically determine the text type (e.g., poetic texts → poetic function dominant). Use dominance to classify texts and to guide stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic-function hallmark: projection of equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The true hallmark of poetry is 'the projection of the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection to the axis of combination'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: poetry successfully combines and integrates form and function; it projects equivalence (similarity or patterning among selectable elements) into the sequence (combination), making formal features salient. Use this to evaluate poetic techniques that foreground pattern, parallelism, rhyme, meter, metaphor/metonymy patterns, and other devices that make form part of meaning. Jakobson also frames this as 'turns the poetry of grammar into the grammar of poetry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and form integration (Sound Shape of Language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jakobson emphasises analysis of the 'sound shape' of language and the acoustic correlates of distinctive features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or compose with attention to how phonological properties (distinctive features, acoustic correlates) contribute to meaning and aesthetic effect. Jakobson's later work (with Fant and Halle) stresses acoustic/phonetic grounding for distinctive features—useful for prosody, phonaesthetics, and spoken-word performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive features and markedness (phonology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary 'distinctive features' as foundational elements of language and a markedness hierarchy of features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concepts of distinctive features and markedness to analyse how minimal phonological contrasts shape patterns in language and verse; markedness can be read as a criterion for relative 'optimization' or salience of forms. Jakobson links these ideas to typology and universals—helpful when comparing structural tendencies across languages or poetic traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phoneme and phonological-system analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of the concept of the phoneme and methods for analysing phonological systems (work with Trubetzkoy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply phoneme-based analysis to evaluate sound systems within a language or text (e.g., rhyme, alliteration, sound patterning). Jakobson's techniques are foundational for formal analysis of poetic sound structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic methods: commutation test, paradigmatic and syntagmatic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods Jakobson used include the commutation test, paradigmatic analysis, and syntagmatic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete analytical tools: commutation tests isolate contrasting elements; paradigmatic analysis examines sets of selectable alternatives; syntagmatic analysis examines sequential combinations. Use them to diagnose how elements differ (paradigms) and how they combine (syntagms) to create poetic or textual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jakobson's typology/markedness/universals as evaluative lenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Jakobson's three principal ideas—linguistic typology, markedness, and linguistic universals—interrelate in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these lenses to assess whether forms in a text align with typological patterns, exhibit marked vs. unmarked choices, or instantiate putative linguistic universals; useful for comparative poetics and structural critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known limitation: neglect of 'play' function
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism: the six-functions model has been criticized for lacking specific interest in the 'play function' of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Jakobson's framework, be aware it may under-emphasize playful, ludic, or game-like uses of language. Analysts/composers should supplement Jakobson's functions with attention to play/performative aspects where relevant.
